summary: Explains how to run LSP ping and traceroute across MPLS tunnels and stitched label switched paths, which RFC 4379 could not fully check. It deprecates the Downstream Mapping TLV in favor of a new one. It updates RFC 4379 and was replaced by RFC 8029.

plainLanguage.summary: An MPLS traceroute checks that a path carries the traffic it claims to carry. When the path runs through a tunnel, or is built from several segments joined together, the routers along the way cannot tell which part of the path is being traced. This RFC adds a field that records those changes so the trace can follow the whole path.

questions: how does lsp traceroute work over mpls tunnels
what is the downstream detailed mapping tlv
what is a fec stack change sub-tlv
subtitle: How to trace an MPLS label switched path that crosses tunnels or is stitched together from several segments.

tldr.problem: The LSP ping traceroute defined in RFC 4379 cannot follow a label switched path across an MPLS tunnel, and it cannot follow a path made of several stitched segments. Each router along the way then loses the ability to check that the probe really belongs to the path being traced.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC replaces the Downstream Mapping TLV with a new Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV that can hold sub-TLVs. One of them, the FEC stack change sub-TLV, records that the forwarding equivalence class stack was pushed or popped at that router, so the node that started the trace can rebuild the path.
tldr.outcome: A traceroute can now cross tunnels and follow stitched and hierarchical paths, and each router can still validate the probe. The document has been replaced by RFC 8029.

today: RFC 6424 was a Proposed Standard published in November 2011. It has been obsoleted by RFC 8029, which is the current mechanism for performing LSP ping over MPLS tunnels. It updated RFC 4379 and was in turn updated by RFC 7537.

sections.title: Why LSP Ping Needs More
sections.content:
The techniques in RFC 4379 outline a traceroute mechanism that includes Forwarding Equivalency Class validation and Equal Cost Multi-Path path discovery. Those mechanisms are insufficient and do not provide details when the FEC being traced traverses one or more MPLS tunnels, and when LSP stitching is in use. This document deprecates the Downstream Mapping TLV and introduces instead a new TLV that is more extensible and that enables retrieval of detailed information.

The RFC works through a simple case, an LDP tunnel running over an RSVP tunnel. When a traceroute is initiated from router A, router B returns downstream mapping information for node C in the MPLS echo reply. The next MPLS echo request reaches router C with an LDP FEC. Node C is a pure RSVP node and does not run LDP, so it receives the MPLS echo request with two labels but only one FEC in the Target FEC stack, and it is unable to perform a complete FEC validation. It lets the trace continue by providing next-hop information based on the incoming label and by looking up the forwarding state associated with that label. But ignoring FEC validation defeats the purpose of control-plane validations, and the MPLS echo request should contain enough information to let node C catch misrouted echo requests.

The problem extends to hierarchical tunnels and to stitched tunnels, where the segments can be signalled with the same or different signalling protocols. To trace a stitched LSP end to end, the ingress needs the FEC information for each segment. With the mechanisms of RFC 4379 there is no way to convey the change to the node that started the trace, so the procedures of that document do not make it possible for the ingress node to know that tunnelling has occurred, to trace the path of the tunnel, or to trace the path of stitched LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router along a path checks that the probe belongs to the path. Inside a tunnel the probe carries two labels but only one description of the path, so the router in the middle cannot do that check and the trace loses accuracy.

sections.title: The Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV
sections.content:
In many cases there is a need to associate additional data in the MPLS echo reply, and in most cases the additional data needs to be associated on a per-downstream-neighbour basis. The MPLS echo reply currently contains one Downstream Mapping TLV per downstream neighbour, but that format is not extensible, so it is not possible to associate more information with a downstream neighbour. This document defines a new extensible format, the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV, with type value 20, and adds a Downstream FEC stack change sub-TLV to it.

The Downstream Detailed Mapping object is a TLV that MAY be included in an MPLS echo request, and only one may appear in an echo request. Its presence is a request that Downstream Detailed Mapping objects be included in the MPLS echo reply. If the replying router is the destination of the FEC, a Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV SHOULD NOT be included in the echo reply. Otherwise the replying router SHOULD include one for each interface over which the FEC could be forwarded.

The format is derived from the Downstream Mapping TLV format. The key change is that variable length and optional fields have been converted into sub-TLVs, and the fields have the same use and meaning as in RFC 4379. The MTU is the size in octets of the largest MPLS frame, including the label stack, that fits on the interface to the downstream router. The Address Type indicates if the interface is numbered or unnumbered and also determines the length of the Downstream IP Address and Downstream Interface fields. The DS Flags field is a bit vector of various flags. IPv4 addresses and interface indices are encoded in 4 octets and IPv6 addresses in 16 octets.

The Return Code is set to zero by the sender, and the receiver can set it to one of the values in the Return Codes sub-registry. If the receiver sets a non-zero Return Code in the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV, it MUST also set the Return Code field in the echo reply header to the value that means the detailed mapping TLV holds the code. The Return Subcode is set to zero by the sender and is filled in with the stack-depth for those codes that specify the stack-depth; for all other codes it MUST be set to zero. The Sub-tlv Length is the total length in bytes of the sub-TLVs associated with this TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The new field says which interface the path goes out of, how big a frame fits there, and what the reply status is for that interface. What is new is that it can hold extra sub-fields, so it can grow later without changing the format.

sections.title: The FEC Stack Change Sub-TLV
sections.content:
A router MUST include the FEC stack change sub-TLV when the downstream node in the echo reply has a different FEC stack than the FEC stack received in the echo request, and one or more such sub-TLVs MAY be present. The sub-TLV holds an Operation Type, an Address Type, a FEC-tlv length, a Reserved field that MUST be set to zero, a Remote Peer Address of 0, 4 or 16 octets, and the FEC TLV itself. The two operation types are 1 for Push and 2 for Pop.

The Address Type indicates the remote peer's address type and determines the length of the peer address: 0 for Unspecified with length 0, 1 for IPv4 with length 4, and 2 for IPv6 with length 16. The address type MAY be different from the one in the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV, which can happen when the LSP goes over a tunnel of a different address family, and MAY be set to Unspecified if the peer address is unavailable or the transit router does not wish to provide it for security or administrative reasons.

The remote peer address specifies the remote peer that is the next hop for the FEC being currently traced. If the operation type is PUSH it is the address of the peer from which the FEC being pushed was learned. If the operation type is POP it MAY be set to Unspecified, though for upstream-assigned labels a POP will have the upstream node that assigned the label and this SHOULD be included.

The FEC TLV is present only when the FEC-tlv length field is non-zero. It specifies the FEC associated with the stack change operation, contains exactly one FEC from the list in RFC 4379, and MUST be included when the operation type is PUSH. A Nil FEC MAY be associated with a PUSH operation if the responding router wishes to hide the details of the FEC being pushed.

The operation rules are strict. A FEC stack change sub-TLV containing a PUSH operation MUST NOT be followed by one containing a POP operation. One or more POP operations MAY be followed by one or more PUSH operations. One sub-TLV MUST be included per FEC stack change, so if two labels are going to be pushed, one sub-TLV MUST be included for each FEC. A FEC splice, where one FEC ends and another begins, MUST be performed by including a POP sub-TLV followed by a PUSH sub-TLV. And a Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV containing only one FEC stack change sub-TLV with a Pop operation is equivalent to IS_EGRESS, Return Code 3, for the outermost FEC in the stack, so the ingress router performing the traceroute MUST treat such a case as an IS_EGRESS for the outermost FEC.
sections.plainLanguage: This sub-field says the path changed here: one description of the path was pushed on and another was popped off. Pushes always come before pops, and a pop on its own means the path has reached its end.

sections.title: The Procedures at Each Node
sections.content:
A transit node knows when the FEC being traced is going to enter a tunnel at that node, so it knows about the new outer FEC. All transit nodes that are the origination point of a new tunnel SHOULD add the FEC stack change sub-TLV to the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV in the echo reply, one sub-TLV of operation type PUSH per new tunnel being originated there. The label stack sub-TLV MUST contain one additional label per FEC being pushed, and the label value MUST be the value used to switch the data traffic. If the transit node wishes to hide the nature of the tunnel, it SHOULD use the Nil FEC, whose label value MUST be set to zero and whose remote peer address type MUST be set to Unspecified.

For a stitched path with three segments joined at two nodes, the first stitching node SHOULD include two FEC stack change sub-TLVs, one with a POP operation for the old FEC and one with the PUSH operation for the new FEC, and the second stitching node SHOULD do the same. Both SHOULD set the Return Code to the value that means the FEC being traced changed. For a hierarchical path, where an end-to-end LDP LSP runs over an RSVP LSP that itself runs over another RSVP LSP, the first node responds with two FEC stack change sub-TLVs, PUSH RSVP-B and PUSH RSVP-A, and the node where the outer LSP ends responds with Return Code 3 when the outer LSP is at the top of the FEC stack.

FEC validation is modified on both transit and egress: if the outermost FEC of the target FEC stack is the Nil FEC, the node MUST skip the target FEC validation completely, to support FEC hiding.

At the ingress, if FEC stack change sub-TLVs are received, the ingress SHOULD process them and perform validation. The FEC stack changes are associated with a downstream neighbour and a particular path, so the ingress maintains a FEC stack per path being traced and applies the changes only along that path. A POP after a PUSH, or a POP when the stack is already empty, causes the echo reply to be dropped. The next MPLS echo request along the same path should use the modified FEC stack. On receipt of an IS_EGRESS reply, the ingress should check whether the depth of the Target FEC it sent was the same as the depth of the FEC being traced; if not, it should pop an entry from the Target FEC stack and resend the request with the same TTL, repeating until it receives a non-IS_EGRESS reply or all the added FECs have been popped.

For backward compatibility, the Downstream Mapping TLV and the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV MUST never be sent together in the same echo request or reply. If an echo request carries the detailed TLV and the reply returns Return Code 2, meaning one or more of the TLVs was not understood, the sender MAY resend the request with the old Downstream Mapping TLV instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The router where a tunnel starts says so in its reply, and the router that started the trace rewrites its stack of path descriptions before sending the next probe. If the descriptions do not line up, the reply is thrown away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If a network operator wants to prevent tracing inside a tunnel, one can use the Pipe Model of RFC 3443, that is, hide the outer MPLS tunnel by not propagating the MPLS TTL into the outer tunnel at the start of that tunnel. By doing this, MPLS traceroute packets will not expire in the outer tunnel and the outer tunnel will not get traced.

If one does not wish to expose the details of the new outer LSP, the Nil FEC can be used to hide those details. Using the Nil FEC ensures that the trace progresses without false negatives, and all transit nodes of the new outer tunnel perform some minimal validations on the received MPLS echo requests. The other security considerations discussed in RFC 4379 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator can hide a tunnel from a traceroute either by not passing the expiry counter into it, or by using the Nil FEC so the trace continues without saying what is inside.

CODES USED IN THE FEC STACK CHANGE SUB-TLV

items.label: Push
items.desc: Operation type: a FEC is pushed onto the stack being traced.

items.label: Pop
items.desc: Operation type: a FEC is popped off the stack being traced.

items.label: Unspecified
items.desc: Address type, with a peer address of 0 octets.

items.label: IPv4
items.desc: Address type, with a peer address of 4 octets.

items.label: IPv6
items.desc: Address type, with a peer address of 16 octets.

viz.caption: WHAT THE STITCHING NODE REPORTS IN EACH CASE

cells: Two: one POP for the old FEC and one PUSH for the new FEC.
Two PUSHes at the first node; Return Code 3 at the node where the outer LSP ends.
Three at the stitching node: one POP for the old FEC followed by two PUSHes.
